title: My First Homelab Setup
description: A comprehensive documentation of my first homelab setup using a G3 800 mini PC, Proxmox, and Tailscale.
author: Adamson Buliboli
contentHtml:
Why I Started a Homelab

I’ve always wanted a personal environment to experiment with virtualization, networking, and different OS setups without affecting my main PC. A homelab gives me a sandbox to:

  • Learn server administration and networking.
  • Test different operating systems and software safely.
  • Explore remote access solutions like Tailscale.
  • Keep costs low while having a manageable footprint at home.

Buying My First Homelab Mini PC

After researching options, I purchased a used HP EliteDesk Mini G3 800 from Facebook Marketplace for $150 AUD. It offered great value and compact form factor:

  • Model: HP EliteDesk Mini G3 800
  • CPU: Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-6500T CPU @ 2.50GHz
  • RAM: 16GB DDR4
  • Storage: 512GB SSD
  • Ports: 4x USB 3.0, 2x DisplayPort, 1x Ethernet, Audio jack
  • Power: Low-power desktop

This small but powerful machine became the heart of my homelab.

Preparing the Installation Media

Before installing Proxmox, I needed a bootable USB drive.

Step 1: Download Proxmox ISO

I visited the Proxmox VE download page and downloaded the latest ISO. The file is around 500MB.

ISO Downloaded: proxmox-ve_*.iso

Step 2: Download and Install Rufus

I chose Rufus to flash the ISO to USB:

  1. Downloaded the portable .exe.
  2. Ran it directly (no installation needed).

Step 3: Flash USB Drive with Proxmox ISO

  1. Inserted a 4GB USB drive.
  2. Launched Rufus and configured:
  • Device: My USB drive
  • Boot selection: Proxmox ISO
  • Partition scheme: MBR
  • Target system: BIOS or UEFI
  • File system: FAT32
  1. Clicked START → confirmed data warning → flashed USB.
  2. Flash completed successfully.

Installing Proxmox on the Mini PC

Step 1: Boot into BIOS

  1. Powered on the mini PC and pressed F10.
  2. Changed boot order to USB first.
  3. Enabled virtualization support and disabled secure boot.
  4. Saved and exited.

Step 2: Boot from USB and Install Proxmox

  1. Rebooted with the USB inserted.
  2. Selected Install Proxmox VE from the boot menu.
  3. Followed on-screen instructions:
  • Accepted EULA.
  • Selected SSD for installation.
  • Set root password and email.
  • Configured network IP to 192.168.1.120 for easy access.

Step 3: Post-Installation Setup

  1. Accessed Proxmox web interface at: https://192.168.1.120:8006
  2. Logged in using root credentials.
  3. Updated system packages and enabled recommended settings.
  4. Configured storage pools and backup location (for future VM snapshots).

Installing Tailscale for Remote Access

To access my homelab outside my LAN, I installed Tailscale for secure remote access without exposing ports publicly.

Step 1: Install Tailscale

I installed Tailscale using the official installation script:

curl -fsSL https://tailscale.com/install.sh | sh

Step 2: Authenticate with Tailscale

After installation, I authenticated with my Tailscale account:

sudo tailscale up

This command provided a login URL in the terminal. I opened the URL in my browser and logged into my Tailscale account.

Step 3: Verify Connection

I confirmed that my Proxmox host appeared in the Tailscale network:

tailscale status

This displayed my host’s Tailscale IP address (in the 100.x.x.x range) and other connected devices.

Planning and Creating VMs

With Proxmox and Tailscale configured, I plan to run multiple VMs to explore different systems:

  • Windows 10/11: For testing applications and software.
  • Linux (Ubuntu/Debian): For learning server administration and networking.
  • NAS VM: For file storage and backups.

Each VM will have assigned CPU, RAM, and storage, optimized for my mini PC’s specs.

Lessons Learned

Through this setup process, I gained valuable insights:

  • BIOS Configuration: Always double-check that virtualization is enabled in BIOS.
  • USB Flashing: Rufus makes the process straightforward, but ensure the ISO size matches your USB drive capacity.
  • Static IP: Choosing a memorable static IP (like 192.168.1.120) simplifies future access and management.
  • Remote Access: Tailscale is far easier than manual port-forwarding for secure remote access to your homelab.
  • Documentation: Following the official Proxmox documentation ensures best practices and stability.

Conclusion

Building my first homelab with a HP EliteDesk Mini G3 800, Proxmox, and Tailscale has been an exciting journey. The setup is now complete and ready for creating and managing virtual machines. This foundation will allow me to experiment with different technologies, learn system administration, and explore virtualization without the complexity or cost of traditional server setups.

Whether you’re interested in starting your own homelab or expanding an existing setup, I hope this guide has provided useful insights and practical steps to follow.

title: Installing Windows Server on VirtualBox for a Lab
description: Step-by-step guide to installing Windows Server on VirtualBox, setting up a base VM for lab environments.
author: Adamson Buliboli
contentHtml:
Why Install Windows Server on a Virtual Machine

Installing Windows Server on VirtualBox allows you to:

  • Experiment with server administration in a safe environment.
  • Test networking and domain features without affecting your main PC.
  • Prepare a base server VM for future labs, such as Active Directory setups.

Step 1 — Download and Install VirtualBox

  1. Go to the VirtualBox website and download the installer for Windows Hosts.

  1. Install VirtualBox on your PC following the installer prompts.

Step 2 — Create a New Virtual Machine

  1. Open VirtualBox and click New.

  1. Locate your Windows Server ISO, select it, and configure VM requirements:
  • Name: DC01 (or your preferred server name)
  • Type: Microsoft Windows
  • Version: Windows Server 2022 / 2025 (64-bit)
  • RAM: 4–8 GB recommended
  • Disk: 60 GB dynamically allocated

Step 3 — Install Windows Server

  1. Start the VM → select language, time, and keyboard input → Next.

  1. Select Windows Server Standard Evaluation (Desktop Experience).

  1. Accept license terms → Next.

  1. Choose Custom: Install Windows only (advanced).

  1. Select the drive → click New to create partitions.

  1. Click OK for additional system partitions required by Windows.

  1. Select the primary partition → Next.

  1. Windows Server installation will begin.

Step 4 — Initial Configuration

  1. On the Customize Settings page, set a password for the built-in Administrator account.

  1. After installation completes, Windows Server launches Server Manager.

Step 5 — Configure Network

  1. Assign a static IP address for future lab use:
  • IP: 192.168.56.101
  • Subnet: 255.255.255.0
  • Default Gateway: N/A
  • Preferred DNS: 192.168.56.101 (self)

  1. Verify the network settings using ipconfig.

Step 6 — Verify Server Configuration

  1. Open Server Manager → Local Server.
  2. Check computer name, network settings, and other initial configurations.

Conclusion

You now have a fully installed Windows Server VM in VirtualBox with:

  • A static IP configured for lab purposes.
  • Server Manager ready for administration tasks.
  • The base setup required for future lab projects such as Active Directory or DNS labs.

This VM serves as a template server for testing, experimentation, and learning Windows Server features safely.

title: Installing Windows 10 Pro on VirtualBox
description: Step-by-step guide to installing Windows 10 Pro on VirtualBox.
author: Adamson Buliboli
contentHtml:
Why Install Windows 10 on a Virtual Machine

Installing Windows 10 Pro on VirtualBox allows you to:

  • Safely test Windows features and settings without affecting your main PC.
  • Experiment with different configurations.

Step 1 — Download the Windows 10 ISO

  1. Visit the Microsoft Media Creation Tool.
  2. Click Download tool now to start creating the installation media.

  1. Choose Create installation media (USB flash drive, DVD, ISO) for another PC.

  1. Select your language, edition, and architecture.

  1. Choose ISO file as the media.

  1. Save the ISO to a folder on your PC.

  1. Wait for the download to complete.

  1. Click Finish once the ISO is ready.

  1. Verify the ISO file is saved correctly (e.g., Windows.iso).

Step 2 — Create a New Virtual Machine in VirtualBox

  1. Open VirtualBox and click New.

  1. Name your VM (e.g., CLIENT01), select Microsoft Windows, version Windows 10 (64-bit).
  2. Allocate RAM (4 GB recommended) and virtual disk (40–60 GB, dynamically allocated).
  3. Select the ISO you downloaded as the boot disk.

  1. Confirm the VM creation and specs.

Step 3 — Install Windows 10

  1. Start the VM → Windows setup will launch.
  2. Select language, time, and keyboard → Next.

  1. Click Install Now.

  1. Choose I don’t have a product key for lab testing.

  1. Select Windows 10 Pro x64.

  1. Accept license terms → Next.

  1. Select Custom: Install Windows only (advanced).

  1. Create a new partition → Apply → OK.

  1. Select the correct partition → Next.

  1. Windows installation will begin.

Step 4 — Configure Windows 10

  1. Select your region.

  1. Choose I don’t have internet (host-only lab setup).
    (If you want internet, select NAT instead.)

  1. Continue with limited setup.

  1. Enter the username (e.g., User01) for the local account.

  1. Turn off all privacy settings → Accept.

  1. Skip Cortana setup → Not now.

  1. Windows prepares your environment.

  1. Finally, you’ll reach the Windows 10 desktop.

Conclusion

You now have a fully installed Windows 10 Pro VM in VirtualBox. The VM can be used to:

  • Test Windows features and settings in a safe environment.
  • Install and experiment with applications without affecting your main PC.
  • Learn and practice Windows configuration and troubleshooting.

This VM also serves as a template for creating additional Windows VMs for testing,

title: Setting Up Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) on Windows Server
description: Step-by-step guide to installing Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS), promoting a Domain Controller, and joining a Windows 10 client to the domain.
author: Adamson Buliboli
contentHtml:
Why Set Up Active Directory in a Lab

Setting up Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) in a virtualized environment is one of the best ways to learn Windows Server administration. This lab allows you to:

  • Practice domain creation and management.
  • Understand authentication and centralized user administration.
  • Connect a Windows 10 client to a domain.
  • Prepare for more advanced topics like Group Policy, DNS, and user management.

This setup uses a Windows Server VM as the Domain Controller (DC) and a Windows 10 VM as the domain client.

Step 1 — Install the AD DS Role on Windows Server

  1. Open Server Manager. On the dashboard, click Add roles and features.

  1. Select Role-based or feature-based installation.

  1. Select your Windows Server from the server pool → Next.

  1. Under Server Roles, select Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) → click Add Features.

  1. Review and confirm your selections → click Install.

  1. Installation progress will appear.

Step 2 — Promote the Server to a Domain Controller

  1. After installation, click the flag icon in Server Manager.

  1. Select Promote this server to a domain controller.

  1. Under Deployment Configuration, choose Add a new forest and enter the root domain name: lab.local

  1. For Domain Controller Options, choose:
  • Forest functional level: Windows Server 2016
  • Domain functional level: Windows Server 2016
  • Ensure DNS server is checked
  • Set a DSRM password
    Then click Next.

  1. Leave NetBIOS domain name at its default → Next.

  1. Accept the default paths → Next.

  1. Prerequisites check will run → click Install.

  1. The server will install AD DS and reboot.

Step 3 — Verify AD DS Installation

  1. After reboot, Server Manager now shows AD DS on the left panel.

  1. Open Active Directory Users and Computers.
    Your domain lab.local should now appear.

Your Domain Controller is now fully operational.

Step 4 — Configure the Windows 10 Client

Assign a Static IP Address

Configure the Windows 10 client with the following static IP:

-IP Address: 192.168.56.20 -Subnet Mask: 255.255.255.0 -Default Gateway: (leave blank) -DNS Server: 192.168.56.101

  1. Verify the updated network settings using: ipconfig /all

Step 5 — Join Windows 10 Client to the Domain

  1. Change the computer name to Client01 and join the domain lab.local.

  1. A credential prompt will appear. Enter the Administrator account from the Domain Controller.

  1. You should see the confirmation message:

  1. Restart the computer and log in using: lab\Administrator

  1. Windows will prepare the profile.

  1. Confirm domain login and network configuration:

ipconfig whoami

The output should show:

  • The correct IP address
  • Logged in as lab\Administrator

Conclusion

You now have a fully working Active Directory Domain Controller and a Windows 10 client joined to the domain. With this setup, you can begin exploring:

  • User and group management
  • Organizational Units (OUs)
  • Group Policy
  • DNS configuration
  • Authentication and permissions
  • Additional roles such as DHCP, File Services, and Certificate Services

This foundational lab environment is a major step toward understanding Windows Server administration and enterprise network management. From here, you can continue building your homelab into a more advanced infrastructure.

title: Managing Users in Active Directory
description: Step-by-step guide on creating, resetting, disabling, enabling, and deleting Active Directory users using ADUC and a Windows 10 client.
author: Adamson Buliboli
contentHtml:
Why Learn User Management in Active Directory

Managing user accounts is one of the most essential responsibilities of a Windows Server administrator.
This guide walks through:

  • Creating a user
  • First-time login on Windows 10
  • Resetting passwords
  • Disabling and enabling accounts
  • Deleting users and seeing the authentication outcome

Each step includes screenshots for clear documentation and learning.

Note: This is a detailed post with many screenshots and multiple sections.
To navigate quickly, use your browser’s search function (Ctrl + F or Cmd + F) and look for keywords such as create, reset, enable, disable, or delete depending on the task you want to review.

Part 1 — Creating a User in Active Directory

Step 1 — Create an Organizational Unit (OU)

  1. Open Active Directory Users and Computers.
    Navigate to lab.local → New → Organizational Unit.

  1. Name the OU LabUsers and click OK.

Step 2 — Create a New User Inside the OU

  1. Click LabUsers → right-click the whitespace → New → User.

  1. Fill in the user details, including User logon name → Next.

  1. Set a temporary password.
    Enable User must change password at next logon → Next.

  1. Review the summary → Finish.

  1. Refresh ADUC. The new user appears with type User.

Step 3 — First-Time Login on Windows 10

  1. On the Windows 10 client, attempt to log in using the newly created username.

  1. Because the password must be changed, Windows prompts for a new one.

  1. Enter and confirm the new password.

  1. Password change success message appears.

  1. The desktop loads normally.

Part 2 — Resetting a User Password in Active Directory

Password resets are one of the most common administrative tasks in any environment.
These steps demonstrate how to reset a user’s password and what happens during login after the reset.

Step 1 — Locate the User in ADUC

  1. Open Active Directory Users and Computers → navigate to:
    lab.local → LabUsers

  1. Select the user who needs a password reset.

Step 2 — Reset the Password

  1. Right-click the user → Reset Password.

  1. Enter a new temporary password.
    Check User must change password at next logon → OK.

  1. A confirmation message appears.

Step 3 — First Login After Reset

  1. On the Windows 10 client, enter the new temporary password.

  1. Windows prompts for a new password.

  1. Password change completes successfully.

  1. Desktop loads normally after successful authentication.

Part 3 — Disabling and Enabling a User Account

Disabling a user account is useful when someone leaves temporarily, violates policy, or should lose access without being deleted.
This section demonstrates how disabling affects login attempts and how re-enabling restores access.

Step 1 — Locate the User

  1. In Active Directory Users and Computers, navigate to:
    lab.local → LabUsers

  1. Select the user account.

Step 2 — Disable the Account

  1. Right-click the user → Disable Account.

  1. A confirmation message appears.

Step 3 — Attempt Login on Windows 10

  1. On the client PC, attempt to log in with the disabled user.
    Windows shows the message:

“Your account has been disabled. Please see your system administrator.”

Step 4 — Enable the Account Again

  1. Return to ADUC → right-click the user → Enable Account.

  1. A confirmation message appears.

Step 5 — Login Works After Re-enabling

  1. On the Windows 10 client, log in again.
    This time it successfully loads the profile.

  1. The user reaches the Windows desktop.

Part 4 — Deleting a User from Active Directory

Deleting a user permanently removes their account from the domain.
This section shows how deletion works and what happens when the user attempts to sign in afterward.

Step 1 — Locate the User in the OU

  1. Open Active Directory Users and Computers → navigate to:
    lab.local → LabUsers

  1. Select the user you want to delete.

Step 2 — Delete the User

  1. Right-click the user → Delete.

  1. A confirmation prompt appears → click Yes.

Step 3 — Verify Deletion

  1. The user no longer appears inside the OU.

Step 4 — Login Attempt After Deletion

  1. If the deleted user attempts to sign in on Windows 10, Windows shows:

“The password is incorrect.”

  1. Using Other User, attempting to sign in again shows:

“The username or password is incorrect.”

  1. Authentication fails because the AD account no longer exists.

Conclusion

You have now completed the core user management tasks inside Active Directory, including:

  • Creating organizational units (OUs)
  • Adding new domain users
  • Handling first-time logins and password changes
  • Resetting passwords using ADUC
  • Disabling and enabling accounts
  • Deleting accounts and observing authentication behavior on a Windows client

These actions form the foundation of daily Active Directory administration.
By practicing within your homelab, you build real hands-on experience with tools and workflows used in production environments.

From here, you can explore:

  • Group Policy Objects (GPOs)
  • User profile management
  • Folder redirection and permissions
  • Multi-user organizational structures
  • Automation with PowerShell

Your AD DS lab is now ready for advanced Windows Server learning and future projects.

title: Splunk Stage 01 — First SIEM Lab for Security+
description: While studying for Security+, I stood up Splunk on a Proxmox Ubuntu VM, ingested auth.log, and searched a deliberate failed SSH login.
author: Adamson Buliboli
contentHtml:
Why This Lab

While studying for CompTIA Security+, I kept seeing SIEM tools mentioned — especially Splunk. Reading about log analysis is one thing. I wanted to actually install it, feed it real logs, and hunt for an event myself.

So Stage 01 was simple on purpose:

  • Spin up a Linux VM in my homelab
  • Install Splunk Enterprise
  • Ingest /var/log/auth.log
  • Generate a failed SSH login
  • Find that event with a search

Step 1 — Download Splunk Enterprise

  1. Download Splunk Enterprise 10.6.0.5 for Linux from the Splunk download page.

Step 2 — Create the VM in Proxmox

  1. Create a new Proxmox VM named Splunk (VMID 102) with:
  • OS: Ubuntu 24.04.3 Server
  • CPU: 2 cores
  • RAM: 4 GB
  • Disk: 40 GB on local-lvm
  • Network: virtio on vmbr0

Step 3 — Install Tailscale

  1. After Ubuntu is up, join the VM to Tailscale for secure remote access:
tailscale up

Step 4 — Install Splunk

  1. Install the .deb package:
dpkg -i /home/adamson/splunk-10.6.0.5-86587d4e3b27-linux-amd64.deb

  1. Start Splunk and create the admin password during first-time setup.

Classic IT moment: after install, the Splunk web UI would not come up on port 8000. I checked the service, waited, refreshed, questioned my life choices — and then it just started working. No dramatic fix. Welcome to IT.

Step 5 — Open the Web UI

  1. Open Splunk Web and sign in with the admin account created at install.

Step 6 — Monitor /var/log/auth.log

  1. In Add Data, set up a continuous file monitor with:
  • Path: /var/log/auth.log
  • Sourcetype: linux_secure
  • Host: splunk
  • Index: default

Step 7 — Generate a Failed Login

  1. From PowerShell on my Windows PC, force a password-based SSH attempt. I already have SSH keys saved, so pubkey auth is disabled for this test:
ssh -o PreferredAuthentications=password -o PubkeyAuthentication=no adamson@splunk
  1. Enter the wrong password on purpose so sshd writes a Failed password event to auth.log.

Step 8 — Search for the Event

  1. In Splunk Search, run:
index=* source="/var/log/auth.log" "Failed password"

  1. Confirm the failed SSH attempt appears — along with a later sudo grep check run on the host.

What I Got Out of It

  • Hands-on Splunk install on a real Ubuntu lab VM
  • Log ingestion from auth.log
  • A tiny detection loop: create event → search → confirm
  • A reminder that sometimes the “fix” is wait five minutes and try again

Good foundation for Security+ concepts around monitoring and SIEM — and a base for future Splunk stages (dashboards, alerts, better detections).

Command Reference

Commands used in this stage. Full series reference: Splunk commands.

Host setup

tailscale up
dpkg -i /home/adamson/splunk-10.6.0.5-86587d4e3b27-linux-amd64.deb

Generate a failed SSH login

ssh -o PreferredAuthentications=password -o PubkeyAuthentication=no adamson@splunk

Splunk search

index=* source="/var/log/auth.log" "Failed password"

title: Splunk Stage 02 — Forward Apache Logs from Another VM
description: Stage 02 moves from local auth.log to remote data: Universal Forwarder on ambwebserver ships adamsonb.com Apache logs to Splunk over the LAN.
author: Adamson Buliboli
contentHtml:
Why This Lab

Stage 01 proved Splunk could ingest and search logs on the same VM. Real SIEM work is usually remote — agents on other hosts shipping data to a central indexer.

So Stage 02 was:

  • Enable receiving on the Splunk VM
  • Install Universal Forwarder on ambwebserver (where adamsonb.com runs)
  • Forward Apache access logs over the LAN
  • Search real site traffic in Splunk

Same Security+ theme as Stage 01 — monitoring and log analysis — just one hop closer to how production looks.

Lab Layout

  • Splunk VM: 192.168.1.104 (indexer + Search)
  • Web VM: ambwebserver at 192.168.1.121 (Apache + Universal Forwarder)

Step 1 — Enable Receiving on Splunk

  1. In Splunk Web: Settings → Forwarding and receiving → Configure receiving → Add new.
  2. Listen on port 9997 → Save.

Step 2 — Download Universal Forwarder

  1. Download Splunk Universal Forwarder 10.6.0.5 for 64-bit Linux (.deb) — same version family as Splunk Enterprise from Stage 01.

Step 3 — Install the Forwarder on ambwebserver

  1. On the web VM, install the package:
dpkg -i splunkforwarder-10.6.0.5-*-linux-amd64.deb

  1. Start the forwarder and accept the license (set the UF admin password when prompted):
/opt/splunkforwarder/bin/splunk start --accept-license

Step 4 — Confirm LAN Connectivity

  1. From the Splunk VM, ping the web server to confirm both hosts are on the same LAN:
ping 192.168.1.121

Step 5 — Point the Forwarder at Splunk

  1. On ambwebserver, add the Splunk indexer as a forward-server:
/opt/splunkforwarder/bin/splunk add forward-server 192.168.1.104:9997

Step 6 — Monitor Apache Logs

  1. First attempt used the default Apache paths:
/opt/splunkforwarder/bin/splunk add monitor /var/log/apache2/access.log -sourcetype access_combined
/opt/splunkforwarder/bin/splunk add monitor /var/log/apache2/error.log -sourcetype apache_error

Classic IT moment: Splunk showed 0 events. access.log on this host is empty — adamsonb.com writes to a vhost log instead. After checking /var/log/apache2/, the real file was adamsonb_access.log. Always verify the path before blaming the forwarder.

  1. Switch the monitor to the real site log:
/opt/splunkforwarder/bin/splunk remove monitor /var/log/apache2/access.log
/opt/splunkforwarder/bin/splunk add monitor /var/log/apache2/adamsonb_access.log -sourcetype access_combined

Step 7 — Generate Traffic

  1. From the Splunk VM, hit the live site so Apache writes a fresh line:
curl -i https://adamsonb.com/labs

Step 8 — Search for the Events

  1. In Splunk Search:
index=* source="/var/log/apache2/adamsonb_access.log"

  1. Events appear with host ambwebserver and sourcetype access_combined — homepage hits, assets, status codes.

Step 9 — Quick Stats by Status

  1. One extra search to prove the data is useful, not just present:
index=* source="*adamsonb_access.log*" | stats count by status

Over the last 24 hours: mostly 200, some 304, and a handful of 404 — exactly the kind of breakdown Security+ talks about when covering continuous monitoring.

What I Got Out of It

  • Universal Forwarder on a second LAN host talking to Splunk on 9997
  • Real website logs (not sample data) searchable by host and source
  • A reminder that empty default logs ≠ “forwarder is broken”
  • A simple stats search over live adamsonb.com traffic

Next stage: a small dashboard and one alert on those Apache events.

Command Reference

Commands used in this stage. Full series reference: Splunk commands.

Install & start Universal Forwarder

dpkg -i splunkforwarder-10.6.0.5-*-linux-amd64.deb
/opt/splunkforwarder/bin/splunk start --accept-license

Connectivity & forwarding

ping 192.168.1.121
/opt/splunkforwarder/bin/splunk add forward-server 192.168.1.104:9997
/opt/splunkforwarder/bin/splunk list forward-server
/opt/splunkforwarder/bin/splunk status

Monitor Apache logs

/opt/splunkforwarder/bin/splunk add monitor /var/log/apache2/access.log -sourcetype access_combined
/opt/splunkforwarder/bin/splunk add monitor /var/log/apache2/error.log -sourcetype apache_error
/opt/splunkforwarder/bin/splunk remove monitor /var/log/apache2/access.log
/opt/splunkforwarder/bin/splunk add monitor /var/log/apache2/adamsonb_access.log -sourcetype access_combined
/opt/splunkforwarder/bin/splunk list monitor

Generate traffic

curl -i https://adamsonb.com/labs

Splunk searches

index=* source="/var/log/apache2/adamsonb_access.log"
index=* source="*adamsonb_access.log*" | stats count by status

Check real log paths on the web server

ls -la /var/log/apache2/
grep -R "CustomLog\|ErrorLog" /etc/apache2/ 2>/dev/null
sudo tail -n 5 /var/log/apache2/adamsonb_access.log

title: Splunk Commands — Lab Reference
description: Command reference from my Splunk homelab stages — install, forwarder, monitors, and searches used across the series.
author: Adamson Buliboli
contentHtml:
Why This Page

Each Splunk stage ends with a short command appendix. This page collects those commands in one place so the series is easier to reuse when building the next lab.

Related labs: Stage 01 · Stage 02

Stage 01 — Splunk VM

tailscale up
dpkg -i /home/adamson/splunk-10.6.0.5-86587d4e3b27-linux-amd64.deb
ssh -o PreferredAuthentications=password -o PubkeyAuthentication=no adamson@splunk
index=* source="/var/log/auth.log" "Failed password"

UI: Add Data → monitor /var/log/auth.log · sourcetype linux_secure · host splunk

Stage 02 — Universal Forwarder on ambwebserver

Hosts: Splunk 192.168.1.104 · Web 192.168.1.121 (ambwebserver)

UI on Splunk: Settings → Forwarding and receiving → listen on 9997

dpkg -i splunkforwarder-10.6.0.5-*-linux-amd64.deb
/opt/splunkforwarder/bin/splunk start --accept-license
/opt/splunkforwarder/bin/splunk status
/opt/splunkforwarder/bin/splunk add forward-server 192.168.1.104:9997
/opt/splunkforwarder/bin/splunk list forward-server
/opt/splunkforwarder/bin/splunk add monitor /var/log/apache2/adamsonb_access.log -sourcetype access_combined
/opt/splunkforwarder/bin/splunk add monitor /var/log/apache2/adamsonb_error.log -sourcetype apache_error
/opt/splunkforwarder/bin/splunk remove monitor /var/log/apache2/access.log
/opt/splunkforwarder/bin/splunk list monitor
curl -i https://adamsonb.com/labs
ls -la /var/log/apache2/
grep -R "CustomLog\|ErrorLog" /etc/apache2/ 2>/dev/null
